pageData.title: Colonial Australia & Penal Settlements
pageData.titleline: Colonial Australia & Penal Settlements - The History Web
pageData.para1: Colonial Australia & Penal Settlements. Colonial Australia began as a solution to a British problem: having transported about 50,000 convicts to the New World between 1718 and 1775, Britain lost that outlet with American independence and searched for an alternative. In August 1786 the Pitt government announced its intention to send convicts to Botany Bay - a site recommended by Joseph Banks, who had accompanied Cook on his 1770 voyage - and on January 26, 1788, the First Fleet under Captain Arthur Phillip founded the penal settlement at Sydney Cove. Over eighty years, between 1787 and 1868, around 166,000 men, women, and children were sent to the convict colonies; the system applied even to children from the age of nine, and its stated logic was rehabilitation through forced labour - convicts built the colony's farms, wharves, and roads.
pageData.para2: By 1820 British settlement was still largely confined to a 100-kilometer arc around Sydney and the central plain of Van Diemen's Land, but from 1816 penal transportation increased rapidly and the number of free settlers grew steadily - by 1850 the settler population of New South Wales had grown to 180,000. New colonies followed at Western Australia in 1829 and South Australia and the Port Phillip District in 1836. Transportation to New South Wales ended in 1840 amid public demands for representative government, and a semi-elected Legislative Council was established. The expansion of cattle and sheep grazing inland came at devastating cost to Indigenous Australians through introduced diseases, violent conflict, and the dispossession of their traditional lands - a dispossession met by sustained Aboriginal resistance. Gold rushes in the 1850s then transformed the colonies' economies and accelerated democratic reform, and in 1901 the six self-governing colonies federated to form the Commonwealth of Australia.

pageData.title: European Exploration of the Pacific
pageData.titleline: European Exploration of the Pacific - The History Web
pageData.para1: European Exploration of the Pacific. European exploration of the Pacific was the centuries-long sequence of maritime expeditions - Spanish, Dutch, French, and British - that opened the world's largest ocean to European maps from the 16th to the 18th century. It began with Ferdinand Magellan, whose Spanish expedition of 1519-22 achieved the first circumnavigation of the globe, though Magellan himself was killed in what is today the Philippines and only 22 of the original crew sailed the whole way home. Behind the voyages lay the search for the Terra Australis Incognita, the theoretical Southern Continent that appeared on world maps as early as 1508 - for without such a counterweight, many believed, the world would simply tip up. The Dutch exploration culminated in Abel Tasman's voyage of 1642-43, which sailed south of the Australian continent and encountered Tasmania and New Zealand.
pageData.para2: The eighteenth century brought systematic science: French expeditions under Louis Antoine de Bougainville (1766-69), Jean-Francois de La Perouse (1785-88), and d'Entrecasteaux (1791-93), British voyages under Samuel Wallis and Philip Carteret (1767-68), and above all the Englishman James Cook, by far the most wide-ranging of them all, who made three separate voyages to the Pacific in 1768-71, 1772-75, and 1776-80. One of Cook's most important achievements was finally to prove that the Southern Continent did not exist; the Hawaiian Islands, missed by all earlier routes, were not seen by Europeans until his last voyage. These expeditions carried scientists and artists who cataloged new lands, peoples, and natural history, while scurvy and rudimentary navigation made every voyage a gamble with death - and their maps and reports set the direct stage for the missionary activity, colonial annexation, and political transformation of Oceania that followed.

pageData.title: French Polynesia
pageData.para1: French Polynesia. France's Pacific territories were a scattering of archipelagos - the Society Islands, the Tuamotus, the Marquesas, the Gambiers, and the Austral Islands - around the great island of Tahiti, seat of the Pomare dynasty. France moved in through the missionary question: after French Catholic missionaries landed in 1834 and were expelled in 1836, France sent a gunboat in 1838, and in 1842 Tahiti and Tahuata were declared a French protectorate; the capital of Papeete was founded in 1843. In 1880 France annexed Tahiti outright, and the remaining archipelagos followed - the Leeward Islands in 1888, and the remote Austral holdouts in 1900.
pageData.para2: The conquest was resisted at every step. Queen Pomare IV's kingdom fought France in the Franco-Tahitian War of 1844-1847 and bowed only to superior force; her son Pomare V signed away Tahiti's sovereignty in 1880; and in the Leeward Islands the people of Raiatea and Taha'a, led by the chief Teraupo, held out against French rule until 1897. Under the colony the old Pomare order dissolved: Protestant and Catholic missions, the copra trade, Chinese market gardeners, and from 1908 the phosphate diggings of Makatea reshaped island life, and by 1924 Papeete was a small colonial port at the center of France's Pacific world.
pageData.para3: Island society changed around the diminished Pomare court. Protestant Christianity, planted by the London Missionary Society before the French arrived, remained the faith of most Tahitians, with Catholic missions strong in the Gambiers and Marquesas; a Chinese community, first brought for a cotton venture at Atimaono in the 1860s, grew into the colony's shopkeeping class; and copra, mother-of-pearl and vanilla tied the outlying atolls to Papeete's merchants. The ex-queen Marau and the old chiefly families kept their rank and pensions, while Tahitian-language newspapers and the mission presses kept the islands' own letters alive.

pageData.title: German New Guinea
pageData.titleline: German New Guinea - The History Web
pageData.para1: German New Guinea. German New Guinea was Germany's Pacific colony in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, covering the northeastern quadrant of New Guinea with the Bismarck Archipelago and the northern Solomons. By 1884 the German New Guinea Company was administering the northeastern quadrant - in the same year Britain declared a protectorate over the southeastern quadrant, later administered by Australia from 1906 - and it was in the island territories, especially after the imperial government took over in 1899, that most early economic activity took place: plantations were widely established in the New Guinea islands and around Madang, worked by laborers drawn from across the region. The chartered company's rule drew criticism for doing little to encourage colonial investment. The colony matters as the Pacific's brief but consequential German moment, ended by the First World War after barely thirty years.
pageData.para2: Australian forces seized the colony in September 1914, and in 1921 Australian control was formalized as a League of Nations mandate, administered from Rabaul separately from Papua to the south. The planters went back to their copra, the remaining German settlers were deported, and in the early 1920s prospectors began pushing beyond the coasts toward the island's unknown interior, following rumors of gold up the Markham and Bulolo rivers. Thirty years of the German Pacific had ended in a morning's landing; the Australian chapter had just begun.
pageData.source1label: Britannica: Papua New Guinea - Colonization, Melanesia, Pacific
pageData.source4label: ANU: Rabaul, German New Guinea - extracts from Report Imperial Charter of Protection (Schutzbrief), granted to the New Guinea Company from the Deutscher Reichs - Auzeiger, Berlin, 21 May 1885 - Archives
pageData.para3: The colony's people were hundreds of distinct Melanesian societies, from the coastal trading villages of the Huon Gulf to the big-men of New Ireland and the Sepik. German rule touched most of them lightly but harshly where it came: labor recruiters signed on thousands for the plantations, mission stations - Lutheran, Catholic, Methodist - opened schools and stations along the coasts, and German scientists, anthropologists and explorers pushed into the Sepik basin and the Finisterre ranges in the colony's last years, mapping a world Europeans had barely seen.

pageData.title: The Kingdom of Hawaii & Annexation
pageData.titleline: The Kingdom of Hawaii & Annexation - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Kingdom of Hawaii & Annexation. The Kingdom of Hawaii was the sovereign nation established when Kamehameha the Great united the islands in 1795, ending years of interisland conflict, and completed in 1810 with the peaceful absorption of Kauai. Through the nineteenth century the unified kingdom navigated the pressures of the imperial Pacific - while American investors came to own many of the islands' sugarcane fields and successfully lobbied Washington in their interest; Hawaiian sugar exports soared from some 20 million pounds in the 1870s to over 200 million by 1890, and the United States extracted a naval base at Pearl Harbor, which the king accepted under duress. When domestic sugar-beet producers convinced Congress to favor them, Hawaiian sugar was left at a competitive disadvantage, and Native Hawaiians had become a minority in their own islands by the 1890s as Asian laborers migrated to work the fields.
pageData.para2: In 1893 Queen Lili'uokalani introduced a new constitution expanding the rights of native Hawaiians, and the sugar planters used her reforms as a pretext to seize power: US Marines armed with Gatling guns surrounded the queen's palace, and hoping to prevent bloodshed she yielded, while the pineapple magnate Sanford Dole agreed to lead the new government. The takeover divided America - the Senate, disturbed by how power had been seized, delayed the annexation treaty to hear the queen's representative, and President Cleveland opposed what Harrison had favored - but McKinley won the 1896 election as an annexationist, and when war with Spain broke out in 1898 the political climate changed entirely: annexation was resubmitted as a resolution requiring only a simple majority, and passed. Hawaii became a US territory in 1900, its monarchy gone, its sugar economy now inside the American tariff wall.

pageData.title: The Kingdom of Tonga
pageData.titleline: The Kingdom of Tonga - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Kingdom of Tonga. The Kingdom of Tonga was forged by Taufa'ahau, a chief converted to Christianity in 1831 by Methodist missionaries, who became Tu'i Kanokupolu and took the title King George Tupou I. During his long reign Tonga became a unified and independent country with a modern constitution in 1875, a legal code, and an administrative structure, and a series of treaties - including one with the United States in 1888 - recognized Tonga's sovereignty. The kingdom matters because it achieved what almost no other Pacific state did: it modernized entirely on its own terms as a sovereign state, and its monarchy is unique in the Pacific Islands for having been a constitutional monarchy since 1875. The missionaries had not found it easy - the London Missionary Society and a Methodist mission failed in 1797 and 1822 before a renewed Methodist effort succeeded in 1826 - but Christianity became central to Tongan national identity.
pageData.para2: In 1900, during the reign of George Tupou II, Tonga became a British protectorate to discourage German advances, though it kept its own king, flag and laws and was never formally colonized. Tupou II's extravagance strained the treasury, and on his death in 1918 his eighteen-year-old daughter succeeded as Queen Salote Tupou III. Her early reign joined the old chiefly lines by marriage, healed the long schism between the crown's Free Church and the Wesleyan mission, and won the young queen her people's deep affection - Tonga in 1924 a Polynesian kingdom still ruled by its own dynasty, unique in the Pacific.

pageData.title: The Treaty of Waitangi & the New Zealand Wars
pageData.titleline: The Treaty of Waitangi & the New Zealand Wars - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Treaty of Waitangi & the New Zealand Wars. The Treaty of Waitangi, considered the founding document of New Zealand, was signed in the Bay of Islands on February 6, 1840, by Captain William Hobson, several English residents, and some forty-five Maori rangatira - the first of about 540 chiefs to sign - after ground prepared since 1833 by James Busby, the first British official on the islands, who forged alliances with local chiefs. Its three articles provided for the Maori signatories' acceptance of the British queen's sovereignty, the Crown's protection of Maori possessions with the exclusive right to buy their land, and the promise of the same rights as all British subjects. The treaty matters deeply because it remains the foundational - and continuously contested - constitutional document of modern New Zealand.
pageData.para2: In May 1840 Hobson proclaimed British sovereignty over New Zealand, and everything changed: the influx of settlers was so great that land became scarce, and the government bought Maori land at meager prices to sell to settlers at a profit. In 1844 the Northern War broke out when the Ngapuhi chief Hone Heke Pokai - the treaty's first signatory - and his men chopped down the British flagstaff; wider wars followed across the islands until 1872. The British proceeded to confiscate almost half a million hectares of Maori land, some even belonging to tribes that had not fought, devastating Maori economic power for generations - the novelist Anthony Trollope, traveling through New Zealand in 1872 at the end of the war, described what he saw as a people robbed of their future. Twentieth-century treaty settlements would begin the long process of redress.

pageData.title: The Colony of Fiji
pageData.titleline: The Colony of Fiji - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Colony of Fiji. The Colony of Fiji, established in 1874, was born of a unique bargain: in 1874 the high chief Cakobau, self-proclaimed King of Fiji, and the other leading chiefs ceded their islands to Queen Victoria by the Deed of Cession, seeking order, protection, and the payment of Cakobau's debts. Fiji was one of the few places where British rule began by treaty with a reigning local monarch, and the deed remains the founding document of the Fijian state.
pageData.para2: The early colonial government, under the first governor Sir Arthur Gordon, reshaped the islands with lasting consequences. Gordon protected Fijian land from sale, governed the villages through the chiefs, and, seeking labor for the sugar plantations, turned to India: between 1879 and 1916 some sixty thousand Indian indentured laborers, the girmitiyas, were brought to Fiji under harsh contracts to work the cane fields. Their descendants, the Indo-Fijians, came to make up nearly half the population, giving Fiji its distinctive and sometimes troubled two-community society.
pageData.para3: Indenture defined the colony's half-century. The contracts were hard and the plantations harder, and agitation in India and Fiji finally ended the traffic: the last labor ship, the Sutlej, arrived in 1916, and the remaining indentures were cancelled in 1920. Most girmitiyas stayed, farming leased land and trading in the towns, and by the 1920s Indo-Fijians were approaching half the colony's population - a new Fiji growing beside the old chiefly order Gordon had built.
pageData.para4: The sugar economy rested on a single giant, the Colonial Sugar Refining Company, whose mills and towns organized colonial life, while Fijian society was administered through its chiefs under regulations that preserved communal land and village government. By 1924 the colony had assumed the shape it would long keep: a prosperous sugar colony where an indigenous people, an immigrant community, and a small European elite lived in separate, uneasy balance.

pageData.title: The New Hebrides Condominium
pageData.titleline: The New Hebrides Condominium - The History Web
pageData.para1: The New Hebrides Condominium. The New Hebrides Condominium, established in 1906, was one of the strangest colonial arrangements in history: a single territory governed jointly, and separately, by Britain and France. The two powers had watched each other in the islands since the nineteenth century, and rather than let either take them alone, they agreed in 1906 to share them. The result was a bizarre dual system, known with affection and exasperation as Pandemonium, in which two governors, two police forces, two legal systems, and two currencies operated side by side.
pageData.para2: For the islanders, the ni-Vanuatu, the condominium meant the worst of both colonial worlds. Settlers and companies, mostly French, took over large areas of the best land for copra and coffee plantations, while labor recruiting, disease and dispossession had already shrunk the island populations catastrophically. The two administrations competed and failed to cooperate in almost everything: each power's nationals answered to their own courts, and joint regulation was so cumbersome that the simplest dispute could become an international incident.
pageData.para3: Missions were the islands' third power: Presbyterian and Anglican evangelists in the south and center, French Catholic fathers in the north, competing village by village for converts, schools and influence. Around them the old world contracted and adapted - the grade-taking societies of the northern islands, the kastom of Ambrym and Malakula, the small trading stores and the first village copra plots.
pageData.para4: By 1924 the Pandemonium was eighteen years old and set in its strange ways: two flags over one harbor, planters' concessions spreading along the coasts, mission stations dotting the islands, and the Melanesian people whose land and labor underwrote the whole arrangement beginning, quietly, to find ways to answer back - in the churches, in the first cooperatives, and in movements of their own.

pageData.title: German Samoa and the Partition of the Pacific
pageData.titleline: German Samoa and the Partition of the Pacific - The History Web
pageData.para1: German Samoa and the Partition of the Pacific. German Samoa (1900-1914) was Germany's colony in the Samoan islands, born of a scramble that nearly brought three great powers to blows. In the late nineteenth century Britain, Germany, and the United States all traded and intrigued in Samoa, backing rival candidates for the Samoan kingship. Tension peaked in 1889, when warships of all three nations crowded into Apia harbor, until a great hurricane sank or wrecked most of them, a catastrophe remembered as a providential escape from war.
pageData.para2: A decade later the powers settled the matter by diplomacy. The Tripartite Convention of 1899, sealed in 1900, divided the islands: Germany took the western islands, including Upolu with the port of Apia and Savaii, the United States took Tutuila and the Manua islands with the harbor of Pago Pago, and Britain withdrew in exchange for compensation elsewhere. The Samoans themselves were not consulted, and the last independent Samoan king was exiled.
pageData.para3: German rule was brief but efficient. Governor Wilhelm Solf governed with a mixture of firmness and respect for Samoan custom, building roads, plantations, and the famous clock-towered government house at Apia, while the trading company profited from copra and cocoa. The German era ended with the First World War: in August 1914 New Zealand troops seized the colony without a fight, beginning nearly half a century of New Zealand administration.
pageData.para4: The partition of 1900 still divides Samoa. New Zealand's administration of the west soon faced organized Samoan resistance in the Mau movement of the 1920s, while the eastern islands remained an American naval station - two halves of one people separated by a line drawn in Europe. The story of the colony captures the way the Pacific was carved up among the powers in the age of empire, and how its peoples eventually reclaimed their independence.
